cbcPrimary.title: What is a Market?
cbcPrimary.explanation: A market is a place where buyers and sellers meet to exchange goods, especially fresh farm produce.
cbcPrimary.full_content:
# What is a Market?

Imagine a big open space full of **color, noise, and wonderful smells**.

Women in bright kitenges arrange mountains of oranges, mangoes, and avocados.
Men shout **"Ndizi mbivu! Bei poa!"** while weighing bananas.

Some sellers sit under umbrellas, others on sacks. There are permanent stalls with iron roofs and temporary ones made of sticks and polythene.

**Markets are the heart of every village and town** because they connect:
- The farmer who wakes up at 4 a.m. to harvest
- With the mama who needs fresh food for her family’s lunch and supper

Without markets, farmers would have nowhere to sell and families would have no fresh food.
key_points: Markets connect farmers directly to customers
You get fresher and cheaper food than in supermarkets
There are daily markets (e.g. in towns) and weekly markets (e.g. Tuesday Market, Friday Market)
Markets sell food, clothes, household items, and even livestock
Most markets open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.
cbcPrimary.image_alt: Busy Kenyan open-air market full of fresh produce

cbcPrimary.title: Buying and Selling
cbcPrimary.explanation: The farmer brings produce to sell. The customer brings money to buy. They agree on a price and exchange.
cbcPrimary.full_content:
# Buying and Selling

Good sellers wake up early, choose only the **best produce**, and arrange it beautifully.

They greet every passer-by with a smile and **"Karibu sana!"**

### How bargaining works:
- Customer: *"Mango ngapi?"*
- Seller: *"Hamsini kwa moja, lakini nikupe tatu kwa mia."*
→ Customer smiles and buys!

**Honest weighing is very important** — customers hate being cheated even by 100 grams.

When a seller is **kind + honest + gives good prices**, customers become regulars and even bring their friends.
key_points: Always greet and smile at customers
Bargaining (kununua bei poa) is normal and expected
Use clean, accurate weighing scales
Give small gifts sometimes (e.g. free dhania or one extra tomato)
Happy customers come back again and again
cbcPrimary.image_alt: Happy transaction between farmer and customer

cbcPrimary.title: Money and Prices
cbcPrimary.explanation: Every item has a price decided by the seller. Prices change every day depending on season and quantity available.
cbcPrimary.full_content:
# Money and Prices

Prices are **never fixed forever**.

A seller decides price based on:
- Cost of seeds/fertilizer
- Transport cost
- What others are charging
- What customers are willing to pay

### Real prices in Kenya (2024–2025)
| Crop          | In Season (Cheap)     | Off Season (Expensive) |
|---------------|------------------------|-------------------------|
| Tomatoes      | Dec–Feb: 30–60 KSh/kg  | Jul–Aug: 120–200 KSh/kg |
| Sukuma Wiki   | Always 10–30 KSh/bunch | —                       |
| Onions        | 80 KSh/kg              | Up to 180 KSh/kg        |

**Smart sellers check neighbouring stalls and go slightly lower to attract more customers.**

M-Pesa is now accepted in almost all markets!
key_points: Prices change daily and seasonally
High quality, big size, clean produce = higher price
In-season crops are cheap, off-season crops are expensive
Always check prices from several sellers before buying in bulk
M-Pesa is accepted in almost all markets now

cbcPrimary.title: Saving Money
cbcPrimary.explanation: Instead of spending all money earned at the market, keep some aside for future needs.
cbcPrimary.full_content:
# Saving Money

Many farmers spend everything they earn the same day — soda, clothes, airtime.

**Successful farmers separate money into 3 parts**:
1. Family food & daily expenses
2. Farm costs (seeds, fertilizer)
3. **Savings**

### Popular saving methods in Kenya
- Village table banking (merry-go-round)
- SACCOs (Harambee, Kenya Women, etc.)
- M-Shwari / KCB M-Pesa / Fuliza savings
- Locked metal box at home

**The golden rule**: Save first, spend what remains.

Even **100–200 KSh saved every market day** can become school fees, new seeds, or even a cow in one year!
key_points: Save at least 10–20% of everything you earn
Never touch savings for daily expenses
Join a trusted group or SACCO for higher interest
Small daily savings become big money over time
Savings protect you when crops fail or someone gets sick
cbcPrimary.image_alt: Child saving coins in a piggy bank

cbcJunior.title: Market Practices
cbcJunior.explanation: Simple habits that make customers choose your stall over others.
cbcJunior.full_content:
# Market Practices

Professional sellers treat the market like a **real shop**.

They:
- Sweep around their area
- Arrange produce by type and size
- Write prices clearly on cardboard
- Wear clean clothes or apron
- Never argue with customers

They separate:
- **Grade A** → perfect → higher price
- **Grade B** → smaller/slight damage → lower price

Many even help carry heavy loads to the boda boda for free.

These small things make customers feel **respected** and they always come back!
key_points: Arrive before 7 a.m. to get the best spot
Display produce in clean crates or on raised mats (not on bare ground)
Write prices clearly to avoid constant questions
Sort and grade your produce (big, medium, small)
Smile, greet in Swahili and local language, say thank you
Accept M-Pesa – many customers have no cash

cbcJunior.title: Demand and Supply
cbcJunior.explanation: When something is scarce → price high. When something is plenty → price low.
cbcJunior.full_content:
# Demand and Supply

This simple rule controls **every price** in the market.

### Maize price example:
- Jan–Mar (after harvest) → 90kg bag = 2,200–3,000 KSh
- Jun–Aug (hunger season) → same bag = 5,500–7,000 KSh

Same for beans, potatoes, onions, etc.

**Smart farmers**:
- Sell some immediately
- Dry and store the rest properly
- Sell when price is highest → earn 2–3× more!

Never flood the market with everything at once.
key_points: Scarce = expensive, Plenty = cheap
Check last year’s price pattern to plan this year
Store at least 20–30% of harvest for off-season sale
Good storage (hermetic bags) prevents insects and rot
You can make more money by timing than by farming harder

cbcJunior.title: Post-Harvest Handling
cbcJunior.explanation: Everything you do to crops after harvest to prevent loss and keep quality high.
cbcJunior.full_content:
# Post-Harvest Handling

Poor handling = **30–50% loss**.
Good handling = **double income**.

### Steps for maize & beans
1. Harvest when fully dry (maize black layer visible)
2. Shell carefully (don’t break grains)
3. Dry on tarpaulin until moisture <13.5% (bite test: should crack)
4. Clean – remove dirt, bad grains, stones
5. Use **PICS bags** or metal silos (no chemicals needed)
6. Store on raised platform in cool dry room

With these steps → store safely for **12–18 months** and sell when price is highest!
key_points: Dry until grain cracks when bitten
Use PICS bags or metal silos – no need for chemicals
Keep storage room dry and raised off ground
Check bags every month for weevils
Proper storage = sell at 2–3× price later

cbcJunior.title: Keeping Records
cbcJunior.explanation: Writing down every shilling you earn and spend so you know real profit.
cbcJunior.full_content:
# Keeping Records

Most farmers **guess** profit → many actually lose money!

Use a notebook or phone app. Every day write:
- Date
- Crop sold
- Quantity (kg/crates)
- Price per unit
- Total income
- Expenses (transport, market fee, labour, sacks)

At end of month: **Income − Expenses = REAL PROFIT**

You’ll be shocked how much goes on transport or snacks!

**Good records also help you get bank loans** — banks trust farmers with books.
key_points: Record the same day – never trust memory
Separate farm money from family money
Calculate profit at least monthly
Records show which crop makes most money
Banks and SACCOs love farmers with record books

cbcSenior.title: Agricultural Marketing & Value Addition
cbcSenior.explanation: Turning ordinary farm produce into higher-value products that earn 50–300% more money.
cbcSenior.full_content:
# Value Addition = More Money!

Simple examples:
- Wash & bundle sukuma wiki in 5kg packs → schools pay **300 KSh** instead of 150 KSh
- Sort avocados + pack 12 in carton with sticker → Naivas pays **1,200 KSh** instead of 400 KSh
- Dry mango slices in 200g branded bags → sell at **300 KSh** instead of 40 KSh/kg fresh
- Make peanut butter → **900 KSh/kg** instead of 200 KSh raw

**Little capital → huge profit!**
key_points: Clean + graded + packed = 2–4× price
Put your name & phone number on every package
Start small – even bundling vegetables adds value
Supermarkets, hotels schools love ready-to-use produce
Simple processing (drying juicing flour) multiplies income

cbcSenior.title: Price Determination & Market Information
cbcSenior.explanation: Knowing real-time prices in different markets so you sell where you earn most.
cbcSenior.full_content:
# Market Information = Money

A farmer with information earns **double** the farmer who sells blindly.

### Free price sources:
- Ratim App / Mkulima Price App
- Radio market bulletins
- County WhatsApp groups
- Sokopepe iCow Digifarm
- KAMIS website

**Call buyers directly!** Many supermarkets and exporters have hotlines.

Example: Potatoes 4,000 KSh/bag in Nairobi vs 2,200 KSh locally → hire a truck and become rich!
key_points: Check prices in at least 3 markets before selling
Transport cost must be less than price difference
Avoid brokers – call final buyers directly
Join your county WhatsApp price group today
Information = money in farming

cbcSenior.title: Farmer Cooperatives & Group Marketing
cbcSenior.explanation: Farmers unite to sell in bulk, buy inputs cheaply, and access loans and big buyers.
cbcSenior.full_content:
# Power of Cooperatives

One farmer = weak voice  
**500 farmers together = powerful voice!**

Cooperatives:
- Collect produce store grade together
- Sell whole lorry to WFP schools exporters
- Buy fertilizer by the tonne (much cheaper)
- Give loans using produce as security

Successful examples:
- Githunguri Dairy (Fresher’s milk)
- Meru Greens Horticulture
- New KPCU coffee
- Mwea Rice Growers

**Start or join one today!**
key_points: Bulk selling = 20–50% higher price
Bulk buying fertilizer/seeds = 15–30% cheaper
Cooperatives help members get bank loans
Group certification for export is cheaper
Strong cooperatives can even own trucks and warehouses

cbcSenior.title: Digital Marketing for Farmers
cbcSenior.explanation: Using phone and internet to sell directly to buyers all over Kenya and avoid brokers.
cbcSenior.full_content:
# Sell Online – No Broker Needed!

Steps:
1. Take bright photos (early morning or shade)
2. Write: Crop | Variety | Quantity | Location | Price | Your name & phone
3. Post in 5–10 active groups daily
4. Answer calls/messages fast
5. Use **WhatsApp Business** (free catalogue)

Popular platforms:
- Twiga Foods
- Taimba
- M-Farm
- Sokopepe
- Facebook groups

Many farmers now earn **30–70% more** selling digitally!
key_points: Clear photos + accurate description = fast sale
Post every day in multiple groups
Answer messages within minutes
Use WhatsApp catalogue to look professional
You can sell to buyers 500 km away without moving

cbcSenior.title: Export Standards & Certification
cbcSenior.explanation: Rules and certificates needed to sell Kenyan fruits and vegetables to Europe, Middle East, and USA.
cbcSenior.full_content:
# Export = 3–10× Local Price!

Top export crops:
- Avocados (Hass/Fuerte)
- French beans snow peas
- Mangoes passion fruit
- Flowers

Requirements:
- GlobalGAP or KenyaGAP certification
- Phytosanitary certificate (KEPHIS)
- No banned chemicals (MRL testing)
- Cold chain 0–7°C from farm to airport
- Proper cartons with traceability codes

Certified farmers sell Hass avocados at **120–200 KSh/kg** instead of 40–80 KSh locally!
key_points: Export price often 3–10× local price
GlobalGAP costs money but pays back fast
You can join a group for cheaper certification
Keep spray records for every chemical used
Cold truck from farm → airport is mandatory
